options: A contact force that resists sliding between two surfaces
A force that only acts in outer space
The force that pulls objects toward Earth
The speed an object reaches when dropped
questions.explanation: Friction is a contact force between touching surfaces that resists their sliding past each other.
questions.misconception: Friction gets confused with gravity or with speed; it's a rubbing-contact force with its own direction.

questions.prompt: A book slides to the right across a table. Which way does friction act?
options: To the left, opposite the motion
To the right, with the motion
Straight up
It doesn't point anywhere
questions.explanation: Friction always opposes the sliding — it pushes back the opposite way the book moves.
questions.misconception: A surprising wrong idea is that friction helps things move forward; it resists, so it points against the motion.

questions.prompt: Which surface will produce the LARGEST friction with a sliding book?
options: Rough sandpaper
Glossy ice
Smooth glass
A dry mirror
questions.explanation: Rougher surfaces grab more — sandpaper gives a much bigger friction force than ice or glass.
questions.misconception: Smooth shiny things feel 'safe' to some learners; the smoothness is exactly why they create tiny friction.

questions.prompt: Two identical boxes slide on the same surface. Box A is heavy, box B is light. Which has more friction?
options: Box A — pressing harder increases friction
Box B — light things grip more
They are identical
Friction never depends on weight
questions.explanation: Pressing harder raises the normal force between surfaces, which increases the friction — the heavy box grips more.
questions.misconception: Intuition often says light = slippery; in fact the greater the press, the stronger the grip.

questions.prompt: Which example shows friction being USEFUL?
options: Car brakes pressing pads against the wheels to stop
Holes wearing in old shoes
Machines overheating
A sled slowing down too fast
questions.explanation: Friction turns into the grip that brakes use — that's friction doing the job. Wear, heat, and slow sleds are the waste side.
questions.misconception: All friction feels 'bad' to some learners; the same force that wears shoes is what lets brakes stop the car.
